title: The person in between: agents, critics and bookers
summary: Hodes says there are many people who would love the music if they could hear it. He blames agents, critics and bookers.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Well, it got better for you. With the tours of Europe as a single.

Is coming, much better. There's a new age, they don't want to know nothing about what somebody said about anybody. And I've always said, if you can get by the agents and the critics and get to the people, you're home free. I found out doing the concerts that there's thousands and thousands, hundreds of thousands of people that would love the music, if they could hear it.
The point is, how can you get it to them to hear it? That's the whole point. We're not up against the people listening. We're up against the person in-between.

Yeah, that's right. Who's the guy that writes about you? Who's the guy that books you? How do you find out, when you're talking to a booker who was a violin player, never liked jazz, couldn't stand it? Do you think he's going to plug it? No, man, I'm going to plug rock 'n roll, because that's where the money is. Art, I'm sorry, I like you as a person, there's nothing in the world I won't do for you. And unfortunately, there's nothing I can do for you. I'll do

nothing. And this gets to be a big laugh. So you do it for yourself, to the best of your ability. But as you say, it's gotten better. You can play a festival. You can go occasionally to Europe. You get lucky, you do something friendly like you did for Harriet Choice of the Tribune. In return, she turns out and talks to George Wein, you've got to get him one time. So George Wein, who is not an Art Hodes fan, by any stretch of the imagination, gets me because there's some opening he has to fill.
